title: Automating Oxford Nanopore library preparation
summary: A fully automated robotic workflow for preparing DNA sequencing libraries, built to remove a manual bottleneck in synthetic biology quality control.
context: Master's thesis (MEng Molecular Bioengineering, Imperial College London), developed and tested at the London Biofoundry

sections.heading: The problem
body: Synthetic biology designs and builds DNA to a specification, on a Design-Build-Test-Learn cycle that biofoundries run at industrial scale, with robots doing most of the work. Quality control is the gate between Build and Test: confirming a construct was assembled as designed, before anything downstream depends on it.
That confirmation runs on sequencing, and sequencing needs library preparation first: turning raw DNA into a format the sequencer can read. By hand it is slow and fragile.

images.alt: The Design-Build-Test-Learn cycle as four arrows, with design, build, test and learn activities around the outside, and quality control marked in red on the boundary between Build and Test
images.caption: The Design-Build-Test-Learn cycle. Quality control, boxed in red, is the validation gate between Build and Test - the stage automation hadn't yet reached.

list: Time-sensitive reagents, where one mistake costs the whole run

body: So in a cycle built around automation, the step meant to catch errors was the one still being done by hand.

sections.heading: Approach
body: An end-to-end automated version of the Oxford Nanopore native barcoding protocol on a CyBio FeliX liquid handling robot, running with no human intervention from input DNA to sequencing-ready library.

images.alt: The CyBio FeliX liquid handling robot deck, loaded and ready to run
images.caption: The CyBio FeliX used for the automated protocol.

list: ONT was chosen for its cost, minimal infrastructure requirements and long reads that need no fragmentation.
The FeliX takes custom scripts, and integrates the two modules the protocol needs: a heater-shaker and a magnetic separation plate

sections.heading: Building it for a machine
body: Most of the work was translation rather than transcription.
list: Calibration came first: 3µL sits inside the instrument's reliable range and 2µL does not, so anything below that was handled with mastermixes
Vortexing became scripted pipette mixing, and HULA mixing moved onto the BioShake
Steps that relied on a technician's judgement became conditional logic on user input
Dead waiting time became parallel task execution
The deck has 12 positions but only four support single-channel pipetting, so every component needing individual tube access competed for those four slots
Four parts did not exist as standard equipment, so I designed and printed them: a tube holder, a dual-compartment ice box, a waste box and a Flongle adapter

images.caption: The deck: hardware on the left, the slot layout I designed on the right.

sections.heading: Results
body: Three sequencing runs, each one feeding back into the workflow.
list: Run A: twelve short constructs. Barcodes and sequences were each recovered, but never attached to each other, which pointed to a failure in barcode ligation

Run B: one long construct across twelve barcodes. Only five reads above 700bp, but three of those matched both barcode and reference in full (0.98-1.0), confirming the core reactions were functional and the problem was mechanical
Run C: offsets checked and adjusted across every step. All sequences and barcodes recovered, most scoring above 0.95, with the expected barcode-construct-barcode structure intact
Samples came from four research groups, varying in construct length, concentration and preparation method, so the protocol held on genuinely different inputs rather than one tuned case

images.alt: Sequencing read counts and reference alignment across Run A, Run B and Run C
images.caption: Barcode recovery (top) and construct recovery (bottom). Run A recovered reads but never with barcodes attached, Run B yielded almost nothing, Run C spread cleanly across barcodes.

sections.heading: Limitations
list: Dead volume in reagent wells was the most persistent issue. Several early failures were not scripting errors at all: not enough reagent was reaching the pipette tip
Runs A and B used identical end-prep offsets and gave very different yields. Construct A had been prepared with Taq polymerase, which leaves A-overhangs and skips the need for end-repair entirely
The proprietary CyBio Composer environment has no search, version control or crash recovery, which made debugging laborious and ties the workflow to one vendor's ecosystem

Flow cell loading stayed manual. Air bubbles damage nanopores, and the FeliX cannot validate dispensing angle or depth without visual or pressure feedback, so automating it would have risked the run for no gain
